items.title: The cubic formula forced mathematicians to take imaginary numbers seriously
items.claim: Cardano's 1545 formula for cubic equations works perfectly — but its intermediate steps require taking square roots of negative numbers, even when the final answer is a real number. The formula computes real answers via imaginary intermediates.
items.prompt: Why do imaginaries appear in real-answer cubics?

options.text: For cubics with three real roots, Cardano's formula expresses each root as a sum of two cube roots that individually are complex numbers; the imaginary parts cancel in the sum, but cannot be avoided algebraically — this is the 'casus irreducibilis'
Imaginary numbers can be avoided with smarter algebra
Cubics with real roots are computed without complex numbers

items.reveal_title: Casus irreducibilis and the unavoidability of complex numbers
items.reveal:
Cardano's formula for x^3 + px + q = 0:
x = cube root of (-q/2 + sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)) + cube root of (-q/2 - sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)).

When all three roots are real, q^2/4 + p^3/27 is NEGATIVE — so you must take square roots of negatives. The cube roots are complex; their sum is real.

Example: x^3 - 15x - 4 = 0 has solutions x = 4, x = -2 plus or minus sqrt(3). All real.

Cardano's formula gives:
x = cube root of (2 + 11i) + cube root of (2 - 11i)

It's verifiable that 2 + 11i = (2 + i)^3 and 2 - 11i = (2 - i)^3. So x = (2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4. Real answer, computed through imaginary intermediates.

This is called casus irreducibilis (Cardano's term). For three real roots, there is no trigonometric-free, complex-number-free formula. The need for complex numbers is essential, not an avoidable trick.

This forced 16th-17th century mathematicians to take the 'sophistic quantities' seriously. The cubic was the gateway that pushed complex numbers from curiosity into necessity. They would only become geometrically intuitive with Wessel/Argand/Gauss in the 1790s-1830s — but their usefulness was inescapable from 1545 onward.

The quartic was solved by Cardano's student Ferrari (also published in Ars Magna). The quintic, as Galois and Abel showed centuries later, cannot be solved by radicals at all.
items.why: Real-world problems suggest only real numbers. The algebra of cubics shows that even the simplest real-coefficient real-root polynomials force complex arithmetic in their solution. Imaginaries aren't optional.

items.title: Twice as far doesn't mean half the gravity — it means a QUARTER
items.claim: Gravity, Coulomb force, light intensity, radio signal strength all follow inverse-square laws. Move twice as far away and you don't halve the strength — you quarter it. The geometry of 3D space, not physics, drives this.

options.text: The same total 'flux' (energy, field lines, or whatever flows outward) spreads over a sphere whose surface area grows as r^2. Intensity per unit area falls as 1/r^2 — geometric, not physical

items.reveal:
Newton's gravity: F = G * m1 * m2 / r^2.
Coulomb's law: F = k * q1 * q2 / r^2.
Light intensity: I = power / (4 * pi * r^2).
Gravitational and electromagnetic potential energy: U ∝ 1/r.

The common thread: in 3D space, the surface area of a sphere of radius r is 4 * pi * r^2. Any quantity radiating outward (energy, electric field, gravitational influence) spreads over this growing area. Intensity per unit area scales as 1/r^2.

If we lived in 2D, the analogous laws would be 1/r (intensity spreads over a circumference of 2 * pi * r). In 4D, it would be 1/r^3. The dimensionality of space is encoded in the exponent.

In fact, modern physics tests for 'higher-dimensional' theories by looking for deviations from 1/r^2 at very short ranges. So far, none seen down to ~10^(-5) metres.

Applications:
- Move twice as far from a fire: get 1/4 the warmth.
- Move three times as far from a noise source: hear 1/9 the intensity (sound pressure decreases as 1/r in spherical waves, intensity ∝ pressure squared = 1/r^2).
- Stars further away appear dimmer by 1/r^2 — leveraged for cosmic distance measurement (standard candles).
- Cell phone signal degradation as you walk away from a tower follows 1/r^n where n depends on environment (line-of-sight ~2, urban ~3-4 due to obstacles).

Kepler's third law (T^2 ∝ a^3) and Newton's gravity were unified because the 1/r^2 force law is precisely what makes elliptical orbits work — Newton's biggest mathematical victory.
items.why: The 1/r^2 pattern looks like a coincidence of physics. It's actually the geometry of 3D space showing up everywhere. The exponent IS the dimensionality.

items.title: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Diagonal of a unit square has length root 2. The Pythagoreans believed all lengths were ratios of whole numbers. Hippasus showed root 2 wasn't. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned him for revealing it.
items.prompt: Sketch the proof that root 2 is irrational.

options.text: It has too many decimal places

Assume root 2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b squared = a squared, so a is even (say a = 2c). Then 2b squared = 4c squared, so b squared = 2c squared, so b is even. But a and b were lowest terms — contradiction
Because computers can't store it exactly

items.reveal:
The Pythagorean brotherhood (c. 500 BC) believed numbers were the foundation of reality and that all measurable lengths could be expressed as ratios of integers.

Hippasus of Metapontum supposedly proved the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side. Different ancient sources say he drowned at sea — some say by accident, some say murdered by his fellow Pythagoreans for exposing the result.

The proof: suppose root 2 equals a/b in lowest terms. Squaring: 2 = a squared over b squared, so 2 b squared equals a squared. Hence a squared is even, so a is even (say a = 2c). Substituting: 2 b squared = 4 c squared, so b squared = 2 c squared, so b squared is even, so b is even. Both a and b are even — contradiction with 'lowest terms'.

The discovery that not all numbers are rational was a major shock; the Greeks came to call these new quantities 'incommensurable'. Modern mathematics calls them irrationals — and there are vastly more of them than rationals.
items.why: Numbers feel like they should always be expressible as ratios. The very first geometric constructions reveal they're not.
